title: Duality, canonical degree and vanishing above $2g-2$ over any field
statement:
Let $C$ be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over a
field $k$, $g=\dim_kH^1(C,\cO_C)$, $\omega=\omega_{C/k}=\Omega^1_{C/k}$,
and let $\cL$ be an invertible sheaf on $C$. Then:

1. $H^1(C,\cL)^\vee\simeq H^0(C,\omega\otimes\cL^{-1})$, via the trace
pairing;
1. $h^0(C,\omega)=g$, $h^1(C,\omega)=1$, and $\deg\omega=2g-2$;
1. if $\deg\cL>2g-2$, then $H^1(C,\cL)=0$ and
$h^0(C,\cL)=\deg\cL+1-g$;
1. for every field extension $K/k$, the base change $C_K$ is again a
smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus $g$,
$\deg\cL_K=\deg\cL$, $\omega_{C_K/K}=\omega_K$, and the isomorphism in
(1) for $(C_K,\cL_K)$ is the $K$-linear extension of the one for
$(C,\cL)$ under $H^i(C_K,-_K)=H^i(C,-)\otimes_kK$.

proof.text: The projective curve $C$ is proper, hence quasi-compact and separated. It is Noetherian, being of finite type over the Noetherian scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$ (the only ideals of $k$ are $0$ and $k$). Smoothness makes it geometrically reduced, so geometric connectedness gives $H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=k$. Its local rings are regular, and $C$ is integral and one-dimensional by the curve hypothesis. Coherent cohomology is finite-dimensional and vanishes above degree one. Consequently $\chi(\mathcal O_C)=1-g$ and $\chi(\mathcal N)=h^0(\mathcal N)-h^1(\mathcal N)$ for every line bundle $\mathcal N$. The curve base-change lemma, applied with $T=\operatorname{Spec}k$, shows that $C\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth of relative dimension one. Hence $\omega=\Omega^1_{C/k}$ is locally free of rank one.

Here is the line-bundle Riemann–Roch calculation needed below, independently of the parent sketch theorem. Write $\mathcal N\simeq\mathcal O_C(D)$ using the regular-curve divisor calculus, with $D=\sum_x n_x[x]$. For a closed point $x$, that calculus gives $0\to\mathcal O_C(D-[x])\to\mathcal O_C(D)\to i_{x,*}V\to0$, with $\dim_{\kappa(x)}V=1$. As specified in clause (3), the action on $V$ factors through $\mathcal O_{C,x}\to\kappa(x)$, and the skyscraper is the pushforward along the closed immersion $i_x:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to C$. Closed-immersion cohomology and the zero-dimensional support formula give $\chi(i_{x,*}V)=\dim_k V=[\kappa(x):k]$. Additivity therefore gives $\chi(\mathcal O_C(D))-\chi(\mathcal O_C(D-[x]))=[\kappa(x):k]$. Induct on $\sum_x|n_x|$: remove $[x]$ if $n_x>0$; if $n_x<0$, apply the same equality to $D+[x]$ and solve for $\chi(\mathcal O_C(D))$. The base $D=0$ was computed in step 1. Thus $\chi(\mathcal N)=\sum_x n_x[\kappa(x):k]+1-g$. In particular the divisor degree agrees with $\chi(\mathcal N)-\chi(\mathcal O_C)$, the degree used by the base-change node. Multiplication $\mathcal O(D)\otimes\mathcal O(E)\simeq\mathcal O(D+E)$ now gives additivity of degree, and $\deg\mathcal N^{-1}=-\deg\mathcal N$.

source.place: Step 0, Riemann–Roch as proved in the sketch; divisor induction in the unit proof

proof.text: The curve $C$ is integral of pure dimension one by step 1. Apply coherent Serre duality in its integral case, with $n=1\in\{0,1\}$, $q=1$, and the finite locally free sheaf $\mathcal F=\mathcal L$. Its stated perfect trace pairing identifies $H^1(C,\mathcal L)^\vee$ with $H^0(C,\mathcal L^\vee\otimes\omega)$. For a line bundle the evaluation pairing identifies its dual with its inverse (in a local frame $e$, the dual frame sends $e$ to $1$). Interchanging tensor factors gives precisely (1).

Keeping $n=1$, apply the same duality to $\mathcal F=\mathcal O_C$ first with $q=1$ and then with $q=0$. It gives $h^0(\omega)=h^1(\mathcal O_C)=g$ and $h^1(\omega)=h^0(\mathcal O_C)=1$; the dual of a finite-dimensional space has the same dimension, as seen in a basis and its dual basis. Hence $\chi(\omega)=g-1$. The line-bundle formula of step 2 gives $\deg\omega=(g-1)-(1-g)=2g-2$, proving (2).

Suppose $\deg\mathcal L>2g-2$ and put $\mathcal M=\omega\otimes\mathcal L^{-1}$. Step 2 gives $\deg\mathcal M=2g-2-\deg\mathcal L<0$. A nonzero global section $s$ is nonzero at the generic point: in a local trivialization its coefficient is a regular function in a domain, which injects into the function field. The regular-curve divisor calculus therefore identifies $\mathcal M$ with $\mathcal O_C(\operatorname{div}_{\mathcal M}(s))$ with effective divisor. Its degree is a sum of nonnegative integers $v_x(s)[\kappa(x):k]$, contradicting the strict negative degree. Thus $H^0(C,\mathcal M)=0$. By (1), $H^1(C,\mathcal L)^\vee=0$, so $H^1(C,\mathcal L)=0$ (a nonzero vector in a finite-dimensional space admits a nonzero coordinate functional). The formula in step 2 then gives $h^0(\mathcal L)=\deg\mathcal L+1-g$. This proves (3).

Fix any extension $K/k$. Projectivity and smoothness persist under base change; the curve base-change lemma gives relative dimension one. Geometric connectedness persists directly from its definition: for every extension $E/K$, $(C_K)_E\simeq C_E$, which is connected. Since $C_K\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is smooth, $C_K$ is regular by the smooth-over-a-field regularity lemma (which needs no integrality), and $C_K$ is nonempty and connected; the regular-connected-integral lemma makes $C_K$ integral, so it is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve. The field-extension-flat node gives flatness of $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Flat coherent base change gives the cohomology isomorphisms, and the separated flat-cohomology theorem says specifically that the comparison $\beta$ is bijective, since step 1 established quasi-compactness and separatedness. Thus we have the canonical comparisons $H^i(C_K,\mathcal N_K)\simeq H^i(C,\mathcal N)\otimes_kK$ for the line bundles at issue. Repeating this regularity and connectedness argument for $C_E$ over every extension $E/k$ shows that $C$ is geometrically integral. The genus base-change lemma therefore applies, using also $H^0=k$ from step 1; it gives genus $g$. The degree base-change lemma applies to the cohomological degree, identified with divisor degree in step 2, and gives $\deg\mathcal L_K=\deg\mathcal L$.

The canonical differential comparison is $\omega_K\simeq\Omega^1_{C_K/K}$. On an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A$, its map sends $(da)\otimes c$ to $c\,d(a\otimes1)$. Its inverse is induced by the $K$-derivation $a\otimes c\mapsto da\otimes c$: the Leibniz relations show this is a derivation, and the two composites are the identity on the differential generators. These maps respect localization, so glue. Pullback also identifies $(\mathcal L^\vee)_K$ with $(\mathcal L_K)^\vee$: in a local frame both evaluations send $e\otimes e^\vee$ to $1$. The tensor comparison consequently identifies $(\omega\otimes\mathcal L^{-1})_K$ with $\omega_{C_K/K}\otimes\mathcal L_K^{-1}$.

Both $C$ and $C_K$ are integral of pure dimension one by steps 1 and 6, so the integral residue-trace clause applies to each. Use the principal-parts cokernel description of $H^1(C,\omega)$ in coherent Serre duality. A representative is a finite tuple $(\eta_x)_x$ of rational differentials modulo regular differentials at $x$. Its pullback has, for each $x$, component $\eta_{x,K}$ at each closed point $y$ above $x$, modulo regular differentials there, and zero elsewhere. This is the cohomology pullback: restrict the maps of sheaves to each stalk in the residue exact sequence and then pass to its cokernel; the coefficient maps take regular differential germs to regular germs. More explicitly, the connecting class is the extension obtained by pulling the residue sequence back along the tuple section of the quotient sheaf. The connecting-map statement for sheaf Ext identifies this with composition by the extension class. Inverse image followed by coefficient pushout takes that extension to the extension of the pulled tuple, so it is precisely the cohomology map defined by the canonical comparison. The local residue field-extension lemma gives
$$t_{C_K}(p^*[(\eta_x)_x])=\sum_x\sum_{y\mid x}\operatorname{res}_y(\eta_{x,K})=\iota\left(\sum_x\operatorname{res}_x(\eta_x)\right)=\iota(t_C([(\eta_x)_x])).$$
Every original class has such a representative. The flat base-change comparison sends $a\otimes c$ to $c\,p^*a$, so $K$-linearity yields $t_{C_K}(a\otimes c)=c\,\iota(t_C(a))$ for all pure tensors, and hence all classes. No separability of closed residue fields is used.

Finally use naturality of scalar cup product under pullback, viewing $C_K\to C$ as a map of $k$-schemes and then retaining its $K$-module structure. The definition of scalar cohomology is restriction of the scalars of module cohomology, so these are the underlying $k$-linear maps of the comparisons in step 6. The evaluation maps agree by the local-frame calculation in step 7. Combining cup naturality with step 8 gives, for $a\in H^1(C,\mathcal L)$, $b\in H^0(C,\omega\otimes\mathcal L^{-1})$ and $c,d\in K$,
$$\langle a\otimes c,b\otimes d\rangle_{C_K}=cd\,\iota(\langle a,b\rangle_C).$$
Pure tensors span, so this determines the full pairing. A finite basis $v_i$ and its dual identify $H^1(C,\mathcal L)^\vee\otimes_kK$ with $(H^1(C,\mathcal L)\otimes_kK)^\vee$ by $(f\otimes c)(v\otimes d)=cd\,\iota(f(v))$. Under this identification the displayed equality says that the map to the dual induced by the perfect pairing is its scalar extension. The inverses of these isomorphisms therefore also agree, which proves the final assertion of (4).
